claims.text: FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles initially have a solid state and uniform bulk composition.
The premelting-to-melting transition is governed primarily by surface segregation-driven reductions in surface energy.
Reduced surface energy promotes localized amorphization.
Reduced surface energy promotes grain-boundary diffusion.
The proposed surface-mediated effect becomes more pronounced as nanoparticle size decreases.
Surface passivation or pre-annealing makes the proposed surface-mediated effect more pronounced.
Particle size and surface passivation alter the degree of surface segregation.
Changes in surface segregation shift the interfacial energy balance of the nanoparticles.
Enhanced surface segregation in smaller or chemically modified particles lowers the energy barrier for local amorphization.
Grain-boundary diffusion causes localized amorphous regions to progressively coalesce into a fully molten state.
Smaller nanoparticles will have a lower premelting onset temperature than larger untreated nanoparticles.
Passivated nanoparticles will have a lower premelting onset temperature than untreated nanoparticles.
Smaller or passivated nanoparticles will exhibit a more gradual melting progression than untreated, larger nanoparticles.
The untreated baseline has a phase-transition onset temperature predicted by conventional bulk thermodynamics.
Changes in ambient gas composition can introduce alternative melting pathways.
Excessive nanoparticle agglomeration can introduce alternative melting pathways.
